extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in natural theology and astronomy (educated laypersons and students)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and presenting astronomical observations and physical/geomtrical facts (stars, planetary sizes, velocities, orbits, planes, ellipses) as premises in an argument for a Creator; includes refutations of vortex hypotheses and demonstrations of the need for a central directing force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innumerability of the stars
rubrics_metrics.description: The Number of the Stars is not only made as great, but likewise as innumerable as the Sands of the Sea (scriptural claim), and modern telescopes show vastly more stars than naked-eye counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telescopic observations (Milky Way, Magellanic Clouds, Huygens, Hevelius, Halley) reveal many more stars than ancient catalogues (Hipparchus' 1026, expanded to 1888). The more improved the telescopes, the more stars are seen; thus stars are effectively uncountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stars differ in magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: It is perfectly unknown whether all the Stars are of equal bigness; some appear smaller either because they are farther or because they are inherently smaller; some have plainly altered their magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations (Gregory, Lib. II Sect. 30) show stars changing magnitude over time; this supports the plausibility that stars truly differ in size rather than only in distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alterations among fixed stars (new/vanishing/states of lustre)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some new fixed stars appear, others that had been seen disappear, and some show variable lustre over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical records (Tycho Brahe, 1572; 1600; 1604; Hevelius; Gregory; Mercator; Whiston) document transient or variable stars and missing previously catalogued stars; these phenomena astonish astronomers and must be accounted for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and appearance of planets as 'wandering stars'
rubrics_metrics.description: Planets (wandering stars) appear to move irregularly (forwards/backwards/stand still) from the Earth’s perspective, but relative to the Sun they proceed forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent retrograde motion and varying apparent motion are observational facts; understanding requires abandoning folk prejudices about sizes and distances and using correct geometrical/heliocentric perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mercury and Venus always appear on same side of Sun
rubrics_metrics.description: Mercury and Venus, being the lower planets, perform their revolution so that, as seen from Earth, they appear always on the same side with the Sun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a consequence of their orbits being interior to Earth's orbit; diagrams (Tab. XXII Fig. 1,2) illustrate this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not trust pictorial scale for planetary sizes/distances
rubrics_metrics.description: Common figures and small-scale diagrams mislead observers into underestimating planetary sizes and distances; one must divest prejudices learned from crude representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Astronomical figures often show proportions of distances but rarely true sizes; Huygens' scaled figure (Autom. Planet.) gives better proportional magnitudes to inform correct intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planetary magnitudes (Huygens' proportions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Huygens' measurements give diameters of Sun and planets in proportional ratios (Sun ≈110× Earth's diameter; Jupiter ≈20× Earth's diameter; Saturn ≈13× Earth's diameter; etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From these diameter ratios follow volume/mass comparisons (e.g., Jupiter ~8000× Earth bulk); Saturn's ring and satellites described; use these to appreciate true planetary grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Times of planetary revolutions and distances measured in Earth diameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed orbital periods: Mercury ~3 months, Venus ~7+ months, Mars ~2 years, Jupiter 12 years, Saturn ~30 years; distances expressed proportionally to Earth's diameter (e.g., Earth–Sun = 10,000 Earth diameters; Mercury ≈ 4000; Venus 7000; Mars 15000; Jupiter 51000; Saturn 95000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these ratios (and alternate values by Huygens/la Hire) to compute circumferences, velocities and compare orbital scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planetary velocities (comparison to cannon-ball)
rubrics_metrics.description: Planetary orbital velocities are enormous; e.g., Venus moves about the Sun 146 times faster than a cannon-ball; Jupiter moves ≈54 times faster than a cannon-ball.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculation method: compute orbit circumference in Earth diameters and compare to distance traveled by a cannon-ball in the same time, using Mersenne/Huygens' experimental cannon-ball speeds and Earth-diameter conversions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculation method for revolutions and velocities
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute orbital circumference (using semidiameter and circle ratio), divide by period to get daily/annual travel and compare with known projectile distances to derive velocity ratios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume circular orbits for approximation where needed, apply known geometric constants (π approximations) and canonical experimental projectile speed data to get comparative velocities (worked examples for Venus and Jupiter provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Velocity of Jupiter's nearest moon
rubrics_metrics.description: Cassini's measure: nearest moon of Jupiter at ~24 Jupiter diameters with revolution ~1 day 18h 28m 36s; circumference computes to ~1727 Jupiter diameters leading to highly rapid orbital speed (>> cannon-ball).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate Jupiter diameters to Earth diameters (Jupiter ≈20 Earth diameters) to express moon's daily travel in Earth diameters and compare to Jupiter's own daily orbital travel about Sun.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force required to move a planet (mass×velocity argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: The force required to move a planet scales with its mass multiplied by its velocity; Jupiter (≈8000× Earth's mass and ≈54× bullet speed) requires force ≈432,000 times that needed to move Earth at bullet speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume equal density for Earth and Jupiter for back-of-envelope; multiply mass ratio by velocity ratio to estimate comparative force; even accounting for density differences, result is enormous and compelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atheists' vortex hypothesis and its insufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Some attribute planetary motions to a whirling subtle matter (vortex) carrying bodies like particles in spinning water; this evasion fails because it merely shifts the need to explain why the vortex matter itself moves in curves and why bodies do not proceed in tangents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that simple vortices cannot account for observed elliptical orbits, obliquities, distinct orbital planes, and continued precise motion without invoking some directing force or cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orbits lie in distinct planes (not a single common plane)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each planet moves in its own particular plane; the planes of different planets cut each other obliquely (not coplanar), and the moons' planes differ as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diagrams (hoop analogy, Tab. XXII Fig.) and observational data (Whiston, Huygens) to show planets' orbital planes intersect the ecliptic along different lines (nodes) and have different inclinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of orbital planes and nodes
rubrics_metrics.description: The lines of intersection (nodes) between each planet's orbital plane and the ecliptic differ for each planet, the inclinations (obliquities) differ, but each intersection line passes through the Sun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These geometric regularities (distinct nodes, shared focus at Sun) are documented by astronomers and argue against a single common rotating medium as the cause of motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of a central directing force (tangent vs curved motion argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies put into motion naturally move in straight lines (tangents); planets continually depart from their tangents and approach the Sun an amount consistent with a continuous central attraction; thus there must be a force pulling them toward the Sun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sling/stone/tangent example (Tab. XXII Fig. 4–5): if a planet tended to move along tangents AP or GQ, something must continuously draw it toward the Sun to produce its curved orbit; vortices fail to explain this without positing another directing power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orbits are ellipses (Keplerian property) with Sun at a focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations show planetary paths are not exact circles but ellipses; each ellipse has two foci (one occupied by the Sun), with aphelion and perihelion points corresponding to farthest and nearest approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elliptical geometry (string-and-nail construction) explains aphelion/perihelion and supports the need for a central force law; this differentiates elliptical motion from circular vortical motion and is based on repeated astronomical observations since Kepler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aphelia point in different directions (non-alignment of ellipses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The aphelia (farthest points) of different planetary ellipses extend toward different parts of the heavens rather than toward one common direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lack of global alignment among aphelia, together with distinct orbital planes and long-term stability, militates against simple mechanical vortex explanations and points to a directing will or law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cumulative convictions used as proof of design
rubrics_metrics.description: A catalogue of astronomical facts (enormous magnitudes, high velocities, satellites, attraction to the Sun across vast distances, distinct orbital planes, ellipses, differing aphelia, long-term stable order) collectively constitute strong grounds to infer a supreme directing power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text enumerates these as sequential premises (First, Secondly, Thirdly, ... Finally) to build an argument: compare planetary magnitudes/distances/velocities, observe attractions and geometry, note continual preservation without confusion, and infer the necessity of a directing Creator rather than chance or purely mechanical vortices.
